cards.front: **The ten areas of the HCM wheel** — and the mnemonic that orders them
cards.back:
**Walk the employee's life through the wheel — it is H2R in order:**

| Stage | Area |
|---|---|
| Before they join | **Recruitment** |
| The day they join | **Personnel Management** |
| Every day after | **Time, Leave, Attendance** · **Workforce Scheduling** |
| Every month | **Benefits and Payroll** · **Compensation Management** |
| Every year | **Talent / Performance Management** · **Learning Management** |
| Throughout | **Employee Self Service** · **Employee Health & Safety** |

**Recruit → record → schedule → pay → develop**, with **ESS** as the channel and **EHS** as the duty of care underneath.

The deck labels the whole wheel **the Hire-to-Retire process.**

cards.front: **Why are strategic HR processes automated last?**
cards.back:
**Because the underlying judgement cannot be encoded.**

A system can *record* a performance rating and *route* it for approval — but it cannot *form* the opinion. So the software adds proportionally less, and it goes last.

| | First wave | Last wave |
|---|---|---|
| Processes | payroll, records, time, leave | performance, compensation planning, learning |
| Character | **transaction-intensive**, rule-governed | **strategic**, judgement-based |

**Being rule-governed is what makes something both *operational* and *automatable*** — which is why the two classifications line up exactly.

cards.front: **Three common examples of recruitment analytics**
cards.back:
1. **Cost per hire**
2. **Time to fill vacant positions**
3. **Onboarding efficiency**

They measure **money, speed and quality** of the hiring process. *(Attrition is a retention metric — it comes after recruitment ends.)*

cards.front: **Succession planning** — which area does it belong to? And why is it confusable?
cards.back:
**Talent Management — NOT Learning Management.**

The MCQ bank states it as a True/False: *"Succession planning is a part of learning management"* → **FALSE.**

**Learning management delivers training; succession planning identifies who replaces whom** — a talent decision, not a training activity.

⚠️ What makes the boundary slippery: **skill training also sits under Talent Management.**

cards.front: **360-degree appraisal** — what is it, and why does it exist?
cards.back:
**Feedback from all directions** — manager, peers, subordinates, sometimes customers — rather than only from the person above you.

**Why it exists:** in knowledge work your manager sees only a fraction of what you do, while your peers see the rest. **The measurement problem is a visibility problem**, and 360 solves it by widening the set of observers.

*"360 degree performance evaluation is a part of the ERP performance management module"* → **TRUE.**

cards.front: **The eight areas of ERP Learning Management** — mnemonic?
cards.back:
**Walk one employee through one course:**

**Browse** the catalog → **register** → consume the **content** → **collaborate** → be **assessed** → have **progress tracked** → someone pays the **financials** → management reads the **reports**.

*(Course catalog · Registration · Content Management · Training Collaboration · Training Assessment · Tracking Training Progress · Supporting Training Financials · Reports)*

**Only two of the eight are about learning content itself** — the rest is administration. That is the honest shape of an LMS inside an ERP: its value is **managing training at scale**, not teaching.

cards.front: **Employee Self Service** — what does an employee do themselves, and what is the underlying principle?
cards.back:
**Benefits · maintenance of personal data · leave application · accessing pay slip and payroll data · registering for a new training** — *"employees maintain all these data and do all these transactions themselves."*

The **employee portal** is *"a personalizable portal designed for employee communications, content management, and integration to self-service applications."*

**The principle:** the person who knows your new address is **you**. Routing that change through an HR clerk adds a delay, a transcription error and a cost — and produces data no fresher than the day you got round to telling them. **Self-service moves data entry to the person with the knowledge.**

cards.front: **Strategic vs operational HR** — the reliable test
cards.back:
**Strategic processes contain the words "design" or "planning":**
*performance management process **design*** · *compensation **planning*** · ***planning** job roles* · *recruitment process **design*** · *workforce **planning***

**Operational processes are the running of the thing:**
records · leave · time · tax · **payroll** · benefits administration

> **Design it or plan it = strategic. Run it every month = operational.**

⚠️ The three T/F traps: *planning job roles is strategic* (**TRUE**) · *payroll is strategic* (**FALSE**) · *succession planning is part of learning management* (**FALSE**).

cards.front: **EHS** — expansion, and the caution attached to it
cards.back:
**The deck expands EHS as Employee Health and Safety.** Answer that in an exam.

⚠️ **Industry more commonly reads EHS as "Environment, Health and Safety"** — and the deck's own sub-areas (**industrial hygiene, occupational health, hazardous substances**) actually belong to that broader reading. Know both; give the deck's.

cards.front: **The four broad categories under the financial module** — and the question each answers
cards.back:
| Category | Question | Audience |
|---|---|---|
| **Financial Accounting** | *What happened?* — the statutory record | **outside** — regulators, shareholders, auditors |
| **Management Accounting** | *Where did the money go, was it worth it?* | **inside** — managers |
| **Financial SCM** | *Will the customer actually pay us?* | **customers** |
| **Treasury** | *Do we have cash, what is it doing?* | **banks and markets** |

The first two are the classic **external vs internal** accounting split. FA is **legally mandated and format-constrained**; MA is **discretionary and shaped to whatever the business needs to decide.**

cards.front: **Why is Finance almost always in the first implementation wave?**
cards.back:
**Because every transaction anywhere in the enterprise eventually becomes a number in Finance.**

Hire someone → **payroll cost**. Raise a purchase order → **a payable**. Run a production order → **a cost**. Ship an order → **revenue and a receivable**.

**No other module receives input from all the others.**

Hence: *"FM is a highly integrated ERP module — other areas of ERP transactions have financial implications"*, and **the General Ledger is the single point where the whole enterprise's activity is visible in one currency.** *(Which is exactly why Nestlé's **nine different general ledgers** were so damaging.)*

cards.front: **AP vs AR** — which direction is which?
cards.back:
**Mnemonic: A**c**c**ounts **P**ayable = we **P**ay. **A**ccounts **R**eceivable = we **R**eceive.

| | Meaning | Cycle it ends |
|---|---|---|
| **AP** | money **we owe suppliers** | **Procure-to-Pay** — *automates the Invoice-to-Payment cycle* |
| **AR** | money **customers owe us** | **Order-to-Cash** — *payment receipt, credit checks, risk management, customer service* |

**GL = General Ledger** — the book everything posts into: **trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports.**

cards.front: **FSCM** — the three C's
cards.back:
**Collection · Credit · Dispute**

Or, as three questions in sequence: ***"Can they pay, will they pay, why haven't they paid?"***

- **Credit management** — *can* they pay? *(decided before you ship)*
- **Collections management** — *will* they pay? *(chasing what is due)*
- **Dispute management** — *why haven't they paid?* *(resolving the reason)*

FSCM is the **cash side of the customer relationship** — the money half of what CRM handles as the relationship half.

cards.front: **The five levels of MRP II** — mnemonic and what each plans
cards.back:
> ### **Business Says Make More Products**

| | Level | Plans | Capacity check |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B** | **Business Plan** | long-term goals, product lines, markets — agreed by **Marketing, Production, Finance and Engineering** | **RP** |
| **S** | **S&OP** | **product groups** per period — by **Sales and Marketing** together | **RP** |
| **M** | **MPS** | **finished products** per period (typically weekly); **ATP** and delivery promise | **RCCP** |
| **M** | **MRP** | **components** — how much (from **BOM**) and when (from **lead times**) | **CRP** |
| **P** | **PAC** | the **implementation phase** — purchasing + production activity control | **CC** |

**Each level is more detailed and shorter-horizon than the one above it.**

cards.front: **Purchasing vs Production Activity Control** — the level-5 split
cards.back:
> *"While **purchasing controls flow of materials from vendor to factory**, **production activity control plans and controls flow of work through the factory**."*

**Materials coming in · work moving through.**

Level 5 is *"the **implementation phase** of production planning and control systems"* — **the boundary where planning becomes execution.**

cards.front: **Level vs Chase** — the two S&OP strategies
cards.back:
The same variation, absorbed in two different places:

| | **Level** | **Chase** |
|---|---|---|
| Production rate | **constant** | **follows demand** |
| Variation absorbed in | **inventory** | **capacity** |
| Cost paid | **holding stock** | **overtime, hiring/firing, subcontracting** |

**Two quantities that move differently cannot match by themselves** — so you buy the mismatch either as stock or as flexible capacity.

The same trade-off reappears in **capacity planning** and again in **DRP** *(central stock = efficient; local stock = responsive)*.

cards.front: **How is MPS expressed** in make-to-stock vs make-to-order?
cards.back:
| Operation | MPS expressed in |
|---|---|
| **Continuous (make-to-stock)** | **end-items** |
| **Assemble-to-order** | **modules** |
| **Job shop (make-to-order)** | **customer orders** |

**The logic is what you can name in advance.** Making for stock, you know the **product** but not the buyer → schedule **end-items**. Making to order, the **order itself** is the unit — every one is different.

**Customer specific products = make-to-order.** Push it further and you get **engineer-to-order**, where *"every new order has a unique BOM"* — which is why **MRP does not fit there.**

cards.front: **MPS vs MRP** — the one distinction three exam questions all pivot on
cards.back:
**MPS lives at the finished-product level. MRP lives at the component level.**

| | MPS | MRP |
|---|---|---|
| Specifies | **what product** is to be made, and when | **what components** to make or buy, and when |
| Contains | quantities and delivery dates of **final products** | quantity and timing of **planned order releases** |

**Sub-assemblies appear only once MRP explodes the BOM.** Every wrong option in those MCQs is a component-level statement offered for an MPS question, or vice versa.

cards.front: **The three MRP inputs** — and the question each answers
cards.back:
| Input | Question |
|---|---|
| **Master Production Schedule** | *What must we build, and when?* |
| **Bill of Material** | *What goes into it?* |
| **Inventory Status Records** | *What do we already have?* |

**Demand · structure · stock.** Take any one away and MRP has nothing to compute.

*(The deck also lists **Item Master** alongside them.)*

cards.front: **MRP's two outputs** — and why each is two-stage
cards.back:
**They split by *make or buy*:**

$$\textbf{Buy it} \rightarrow \textbf{Purchase Requisition} \rightarrow \textbf{Purchase Order} \rightarrow \text{supplier}$$
$$\textbf{Make it} \rightarrow \textbf{Planned Order} \rightarrow \textbf{Production Order} \rightarrow \text{shop floor}$$

**Why the intermediate stage exists:** so a **planner can review and approve** before the company commits money or machine time. **MRP proposes, a human confirms.**

The PO end of this is exactly where **Procure-to-Pay** begins — **MRP generates the demand that P2P fulfils.**

cards.front: **BOM vs routing** — what does each define?
cards.back:
> **BOM = ingredients. Routing = method.** A recipe needs both.

| | Defines | Drives |
|---|---|---|
| **BOM** | which components, **how many per parent** | **material requirements** and **product costing** |
| **Routing** | the **operation sequence**, times, work centres | **capacity** and **conversion cost** |

⚠️ In the MCQ *"a bill of materials lists the…"*, the wrong option **"operations required to produce an item"** is the routing.

**BOM is "the most important master data for MRP and product costing."** Its other names: **Product Structure**. Its types: **CADBOM · EBOM · MBOM.**

cards.front: **Low-level code** — what is it, and why must it be the *deepest* occurrence?
cards.back:
**The code that drives MRP's planning sequence** — an item's code is **the lowest (deepest) level at which it occurs anywhere in the BOM.**

In the worked example, **C appears at both level 1 and level 3 → its code is 3.**

**Why deepest:** C is used directly in **A** (level 1) *and* inside **D** (level 3). Planned at level 1, MRP would compute C's requirement from A alone — then later discover **D also needs C**, after C's order was already placed.

> **Rule: plan an item only once, and only after all its demand is known.**

Same logic as **topological ordering** — you cannot compute a node until all its predecessors are done.

cards.front: **The gross/net cascade** — reproduce the worked example *(order for 25 A; on hand A=3, B=7, C=16, D=4, E=6)*
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Net} = \textbf{Gross} - \textbf{On hand}$$

| Step | Item | Gross | On hand | **Net** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **A** | 25 | 3 | **22** |
| 1 | **B** *(1 per A)* | 22 | 7 | **15** |
| 2 | **D** *(1 per B)* | 15 | 4 | **11** |
| 3 | **C** *(1 per A **and** D)* | **22 + 11 = 33** | 16 | **17** |
| 4 | **E** *(1 per D)* | 11 | 6 | **5** |

**Two mechanisms at once:**
1. **Net at one level becomes gross at the next** — that is what the BOM "converts (explodes)."
2. **C sums demand from both parents** — and is planned last *because* its low-level code is 3.

cards.front: **MRP vs CBP** — dependent and independent demand
cards.back:
| **MRP** | **CBP (Consumption Based Planning)** |
|---|---|
| **production items** | **consumables, spares, office supplies** |
| driven by **finished goods requirement** | driven by **past consumption and forecast** |
| **needs a BOM explosion** | **no BOM explosion** |

**The distinction is dependent vs independent demand.**

**MRP handles dependent demand** — how many wheels you need is *derived* from how many bicycles you build. It is **computed, not forecast**.

**CBP handles independent demand** — office stationery has no BOM relationship to anything you sell, so it can only be **forecast from history**. Hence **no BOM to explode**, and hence its fit for **class B and C items**.

CBP approaches: **reorder point · forecast based · time-phased.**

cards.front: **Backward scheduling** — the requisition-date formula and the three subtractions
cards.back:
$$\textbf{PR date} = \textbf{MRP date} - \textbf{GR processing time} - \textbf{Vendor lead time} - \textbf{Purchasing processing time}$$

| Subtract | Because |
|---|---|
| **Goods Receipt processing** | material at the gate is not yet usable — receive, inspect, put away |
| **Vendor lead time** | the supplier needs time to deliver after being ordered |
| **Purchasing processing** | your own team needs time to turn a requisition into an order |

**The most-forgotten is the first.**

**Backward asks "when must I start to finish on time?"; forward asks "if I start now, when will I finish?"**

cards.front: **Time fences** — the four zones
cards.back:
> ### **Frozen · Firm · Full · Open** — *the further away, the freer you are*

| Zone | To due date | Change |
|---|---|---|
| **Frozen** | **1–2 weeks** | **none** |
| **Firm** | **2–4 weeks** | **± 5%** |
| **Full** | **4–6 weeks** | **± 10%** |
| **Open** | **6+ weeks** | **± 20%** |

**The logic is commitment.** Material within two weeks is already ordered, delivered, possibly on the machine — changing it wastes money already spent. Six weeks out, nothing is committed.

**This is the mechanism that reconciles manufacturing's need for a stable schedule with sales' need for flexibility** — stability near in, flexibility far out.

cards.front: **Lot sizing** — the two families, and why not simply order exactly what you need?
cards.back:
| Family | Procedures |
|---|---|
| **Static** — fix the **quantity** | lot-for-lot · replenish to maximum stock level · fixed lot size |
| **Periodic** — fix the **interval** | daily · weekly · monthly · planning calendar |

**Ordering exactly what you need *is* lot-for-lot** — minimal inventory, but constant small orders.

**Every order carries a fixed cost regardless of size** — a delivery, a setup, paperwork. So *"lot sizing is primarily for **optimizing** — transportation / packing costs and other overheads."*

**It trades ordering cost against inventory holding cost.**

cards.front: **MRP's seven limitations** — grouped so they are reproducible
cards.back:
| Kind | Limitations |
|---|---|
| **What it cannot see** | ① projects requirements only ② **cannot consider actual capacity, constraints, vendor limits** |
| **What it cannot do** | ③ **no optimization** ⑤ **cannot replan fast enough** |
| **What it demands of you** | ④ **very high data accuracy** ⑥ **high user discipline** |
| **Where it does not fit** | ⑦ **project / engineer-to-order** — *every new order has a unique BOM* |

**④ and ⑥ are the ones that bite in practice** — this is *"Garbage In, Garbage Out"* landing in production planning. **An MRP run on a wrong BOM confidently orders the wrong parts.**

The deck's own balance: *"many of the limitations are drawbacks **in comparison to other products**; in some cases **there may not be better alternatives**. These are **pointers for improvement**."*

cards.front: **"MRP is an infinite planning tool"** — what does that mean, and what closes the loop?
cards.back:
**MRP does not consider available capacity while planning — it assumes capacity is infinite.**

It works **backwards from the schedule** through the BOM and lead times. That arithmetic is perfectly correct and says **nothing about whether the factory can do the work** — it will happily demand 300 machine-hours in a week from a plant with 120.

**Closing the loop:**
$$\textbf{S\&OP} \rightarrow \textbf{MPS} \rightarrow \textbf{MRP} \rightarrow \textbf{CRP} \rightarrow \textbf{Realistic?}$$
**No** → feed back **to MPS** and re-run · **Yes** → execute.

⚠️ **The correction is applied at MPS, not at MRP.** If capacity cannot support the plan, you **build fewer finished products** — which changes what sales can promise. **The constraint propagates upward.**

cards.front: **The four levels of capacity planning** — each paired with the planning level it checks
cards.back:
$$\begin{aligned}\textbf{S\&OP} &\longleftrightarrow \textbf{RP} \text{ — Resource Planning} \\ \textbf{MPS} &\longleftrightarrow \textbf{RCCP} \text{ — Rough Cut Capacity Planning} \\ \textbf{MRP} &\longleftrightarrow \textbf{CRP} \text{ — Capacity Requirement Planning} \\ \textbf{PAC} &\longleftrightarrow \textbf{CC} \text{ — Capacity Control}\end{aligned}$$

**Every planning level has a matching capacity check, and the checks get finer as you descend** — RP asks a rough question about whole plants over months; CC manages machine loading on a shift.

**"Rough Cut" is named honestly** — at MPS level you check only the **critical resources**, because the plan is not detailed enough to justify more.

cards.front: **Why is the capacity mismatch structural rather than a planning failure?**
cards.back:
**Capacity is fixed in the short run** — you cannot buy half a machine or hire a skilled operator for one afternoon. **Demand is continuously variable.**

**Two quantities that move differently cannot match by themselves.**

So the mismatch always costs you one of two things: **idle capacity you are paying for**, or **demand you cannot serve**.

The listed strategies — **overtime, outsourcing, subcontracting** — are all ways of **buying short-term capacity at a premium** rather than owning it year-round. *(The same Level vs Chase trade-off from S&OP.)*

⚠️ And the deck is candid: **"ERP's support for capacity management is a little indirect"** — which is exactly the market **APS** fills.

cards.front: **The four master data elements for PP** — mnemonic and the question each answers
cards.back:
> ### **My BOM Works Right**

| Word | Element | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **M**y | **Material Master** | **what** is it? |
| **BOM** | **Bill of Material** | **what goes into** it? |
| **W**orks | **Work Center** | **where** is it made? |
| **R**ight | **Routing** | **in what order**? |

**What · what-from · where · in-what-order.**

**BOM and Routing are a pair** — the BOM is the *ingredients*, the routing is the *method*.

cards.front: **The material master's four data segments** — and why the segmentation exists at all
cards.back:
| Segment | Examples |
|---|---|
| **General Data** | material number, description, units of measure, weight, volume, product hierarchy |
| **Plant Specific** | MRP profile, production costs, planning data, valuation |
| **Storage Location Specific** | quantities, special stock, warehouse attributes |
| **Sales Specific** | delivering plant, sales text, sales units, shipping data, division |

**Why:** the same material means different things in different places. **Weight** is the same everywhere; the **MRP profile** may differ between plants; **stock** obviously differs by location; the **sales unit** may differ by channel *(singly in retail, by the case to wholesalers)*.

So the record is **one general core plus per-plant, per-location and per-sales-org extensions** — which lets a multi-plant company hold **one material number** enterprise-wide while recording local differences. **Data standardization done properly**, as against Nestlé's 29 vanilla records.

cards.front: **Why is a purchase clerk allowed to see cost price when the works manager is not?**
cards.back:
> *"Information required for purchase is not required for work scheduling. So a **purchase clerk might have access to 'sensitive' information such as cost price, but the works manager may not** — even though in the org structure he is 'superior'."*

> ### **Access follows the job, not the rank.**

That is what a **material master "view"** is for: *what one function needs to see*. It is the material-master version of **role-based access**, and the practical form of Unit 1's *"flat org structure / employee empowerment / **controlled access**."*

cards.front: **The routing example** — and the three jobs one small table is doing
cards.back:
| Operation | Time | Work Center | Function | Cost Center |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **10** | **20 min** | **W1** | Assembly | **100** |
| **20** | **15 min** | **W2** | **Painting** | **200** |
| **30** | **10 min** | **W3** | **Finishing** | **300** |

- **Sequencing** — 10, 20, 30 set the order. *(They step by ten so an operation can be inserted between two without renumbering.)*
- **Scheduling** — **45 minutes** of work content per unit.
- **Costing** — each work centre is **linked to a cost centre**, so time converts directly into cost.

$$\textbf{Routing} \times \textbf{quantity} \rightarrow \textbf{load per work centre} \rightarrow \textbf{capacity check} + \textbf{cost}$$

**This is where CRP gets its numbers from.**

cards.front: **The three production scenarios** — characteristics and examples
cards.back:
| Scenario | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Process Industry** | **batch management, recipe, PI sheets, ERP↔PLC interface** | chemical, oil and gas, pharmaceutical, petrochemical |
| **Repetitive Manufacturing** | **less complex, more stable, long periods same product; material staging, back flushing** | consumer goods (FMCG), electronics |
| **Kanban / JIT** | **JIT, Kanban** — electronic kanban card, kanban quantity calculation | industries using Kanban or JIT |

**They sit on a spectrum of how discrete the product is:** process makes what you **measure**; repetitive makes identical units **continuously**; Kanban makes discrete units **pulled by consumption**.

**Recipe ⟺ BOM in process industry.** **Batch management exists because "chemical properties may differ"** — two batches are **not interchangeable**.

cards.front: **Back flushing** — what it does, why it suits repetitive manufacturing, and what it costs
cards.back:
**It inverts the normal flow.** Instead of issuing materials then producing, you **record the finished goods and work backwards through the BOM** to deduct what must have been consumed.

$$\textbf{1,000 units produced} \times \textbf{BOM} \rightarrow \textbf{components auto-deducted}$$

**Why repetitive:** the product is *"less complex, more stable, the same for long periods"*, so the BOM is reliable. Recording every component issue on a fast line would be pure transaction overhead.

⚠️ **The trade-off:** it assumes the BOM is exactly right. **Scrap, rework and substitutions are invisible**, so inventory drifts and must be corrected by physical counts. **It buys speed with accuracy.**

cards.front: **Kanban vs MRP** — push and pull
cards.back:
| | **MRP** | **Kanban** |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | **Push** — a central plan tells each stage what to make | **Pull** — a stage makes only what the next stage consumed |
| Trigger | the **schedule** | **an empty bin / a returned card** |
| Needs | accurate BOM, stock, lead times | **stable, level demand** |

The card *"triggers delivery **from demand source to supply source**"* — **the demand end initiates.**

**Origin:** **Toyota**, meaning **"visual sign" / "visual card"**; in the **1940s** they were paper notes on a physical board, used *"to create a transparent work process and reduce production waste."*

cards.front: **DRP** — definition, the translation chain, and why it is "an extension of MRP logic"
cards.back:
**A time-phased finished-goods replenishment plan for all levels of a distribution network.**

$$\textbf{LDC} \rightarrow \textbf{CDC} \rightarrow \textbf{CWH} \rightarrow \textbf{Factory}$$

⚠️ **DRP is NOT part of the MRP II flow** — the five levels are BP, S&OP, MPS, MRP, PAC. Requirements translate **inward from the customer end toward the factory**.

**Why "an extension of MRP logic":** its inputs are MRP's inputs with the **network substituted for the BOM** —

| MRP | DRP |
|---|---|
| MPS | **forecast of demand per SKU** |
| BOM | **the distribution network** |
| inventory status | **inventory + in transit + safety stock** |
| lead times | **replenishment lead time** |
| → purchase requisitions | → **stock transport requisitions** |

**DRP explodes a network the way MRP explodes a BOM.**

cards.front: **DRP's objectives** — and the tension inside them
cards.back:
1. **Improve customer service levels** — anticipate demand at distribution centers, **provide finished products at the correct location**
2. **Provide an accurate requirements plan for manufacturing**
3. **Optimize the distribution of available stock**
4. **Minimize finished goods inventory in the network**

**Objectives 1 and 4 are in tension.** *Correct location* wants stock **close to the customer**, spread across many warehouses. *Minimize inventory* wants it **concentrated centrally**.

> **Stock held centrally is more efficient; stock held locally is more responsive.**

DRP is the calculation that decides where the line falls — the same **service vs cost** trade-off S&OP balances at the production end.

⚠️ **SKU = Stock Keeping Unit** *(the deck's note glosses it as "Semi Knocked down Unit" — that is wrong).*

cards.front: **The twelve ERP modules** — grouped by what they touch
cards.back:
| Group | Modules |
|---|---|
| **Inward — supply side** | **SRM · PIM [MM] · Warehouse & Transportation** |
| **Inside — making it** | **PPE [PP] · Quality Management · Maintenance/EAM · PLM** |
| **Outward — demand side** | **Sales & Service [SD] · CRM · SCP [SCM]** |
| **Across — the whole enterprise** | **Financial Management [FI-CO] · HCM [HR]** |

**Money and people are not the property of any one function** — which is why **FI and HR are the two you cannot leave out.**

**SAP names:** **FI-CO** = Financial Accounting & Controlling · **MM** = Materials Management · **SD** = Sales and Distribution · **PP** = Production Planning.

cards.front: **The "earlier vs now" tables** — what single pattern runs through all of them?
cards.back:
> ### **Transaction → decision.**

| Function | Earlier was… | Now is… |
|---|---|---|
| **SCM** | *recording* where stock is | **deciding** what to make, how to route — **optimization** |
| **Fin Mgmt** | *recording* what was paid and owed | **budgeting, consolidation, compliance (SOX)** |
| **SRM** | *paying* the vendor | **choosing** the vendor — auctions, **supplier analytics** |
| **CRM** | *invoicing* the customer | **winning** the customer — **opportunity management** |

**Every "earlier" entry is a transaction that already happened; every "now" entry is a decision about what should happen** — the same **data → information → insight** shift.

Two other threads in the "now" column: **self-service** *(supplier self service, ESS)* and **mobile** *(mobile asset tracking, mobile sales service)*.

cards.front: **Why does the overlap between ERP and niche apps never close?**
cards.back:
> *"**ERP functionalities are getting comprehensive to include the niche functionalities at each newer version, but the specialized products are getting specialized further and maintain independent identity.**"*

**Both sides are running.** ERP absorbs what the specialists proved valuable; the specialists move further into depth ERP will not follow.

So *"they may co-exist within an enterprise"* is **the normal state, not bad architecture** — and it creates a real decision: *"a company has to carefully weigh whether to go for an enterprise app critical to its business, or an integrated ERP. **It is not an easy decision.**"*

**Sharpest illustration:** **EAM and SRM had word-for-word identical "earlier" columns** — *Procurement · Vendor payment · Vendor rating.*

cards.front: **ERP history** — the four decades, and the one-word test for each
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Materials} \rightarrow \textbf{the Factory} \rightarrow \textbf{the Enterprise} \rightarrow \textbf{the Network}$$

| Decade | Stage | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1960–70s** | **MRP** — Material Requirement Planning; *first application of computing to manufacturing* | can I get the **parts**? |
| **1980s** | **MRP II** — Manufacturing Resource Planning; integration with **accounting, billing** | can the **factory** do it, at what cost? |
| **1990s** | **ERP** — all processes integrated; **supports non-manufacturing too** | is the **enterprise** integrated? |
| **2000s** | **Extended ERP / ERP II** — **suppliers and clients** | is the **network** optimised? |

**Each expansion is the previous one's limitation resolved.**

⚠️ **"Supports non-manufacturing too" is the moment the word "Manufacturing" left the name.**

cards.front: **PPE chapter summary** — and the tension in its last two bullets
cards.back:
- **PPE is one of the central ERP capabilities**
- **Has brought in many structured concepts leading to standardization**
- **This is also the place where a lot of "customization" is needed** based on type of industry
- **Proper adaptation of ERP in PPE can result in significant competitive advantage at the core of the company**

**Bullets 2 and 3 pull against each other**, and that is the closing idea. PPE **standardized** production planning — *"MRP II is a 'standard'; all ERPs support it"* — yet it is **where the most customization is needed**, because a chemical plant, an FMCG line and a Kanban cell genuinely plan differently.

> **So the advantage in bullet 4 comes from the fit, not from the software.** Everyone can buy the same package; the advantage is adapting it properly.
